Meanwhile every busy system leans on a cache sitting ahead of storage, because disk reads cost real time. A warm cache absorbs repeated lookups, trims latency, and spares the primary node from floods of identical queries during heavy traffic spikes.

However fast disks become, a cache can still lie. Stale entries drift from the truth held in tables; readers then act on numbers that no longer hold. Invalidation is the tax paid for speed; write-through, write-behind, and plain expiry merely shift that burden, so pick a cache policy matched to the staleness your product tolerates.

Along that path, sizing is craft, not luck: staff watch hit ratios, RAM caps, and how many rows a warm pool can hold; a sharp fall in hits hints at thrash, so many shops shard hot rows across a group of small fast hosts.

Finally measure before you cache anything, because guesses dressed as tuning waste hours. Numbers alone prove the work is done.
